takeaways: Each passive element is defined by its V-I law: v = Ri, v = L di/dt, i = C dv/dt.
Resistors dissipate energy; ideal inductors and capacitors store it (½Li², ½Cv²) and their current and voltage respectively cannot jump.
An independent source fixes its own value; a dependent source is set by a voltage or current elsewhere and must keep its control equation.
KCL is charge conservation at a node; KVL is energy conservation round a closed path; a power balance checks every answer.
A connected circuit needs n − 1 KCL and b − n + 1 KVL equations, b in all.
Series-parallel reduction with voltage and current division solves many circuits without simultaneous equations.
Star-delta and source transformations change the inside of a network, never what its terminals see.
A tree picks a complete independent set of loop (tie-set) and node (cut-set) equations, even for circuits that cannot be drawn flat.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the types of sources with their V-I characteristics, the definitions of the network terms, and numerical problems on series-parallel reduction and star-delta conversion of bridge networks; graph-theory questions ask for the tree, the tie-set and cut-set matrices and the equations they give.

bank.q: Define resistance, inductance and capacitance. For each element write the V-I relation in derivative and integral form, the energy expression, and its behaviour at DC steady state. Explain why inductor current and capacitor voltage cannot change instantly.
outline: Definitions with units: R = v/i (Ω), L = Nφ/i (H), C = q/v (F)
v = Ri; v = L di/dt and i = (1/L)∫v dt; i = C dv/dt and v = (1/C)∫i dt
Energy: R dissipates i²R; L stores ½Li²; C stores ½Cv²
DC steady state: L is a short circuit, C an open circuit
Continuity of i<sub>L</sub> and v<sub>C</sub> from the derivative laws
answer: Resistance. The opposition to current that converts electrical energy into heat. R = v/i, unit ohm (1 Ω = 1 V/A); for a uniform wire R = ρl/A.
Inductance. The flux linkage per ampere of a coil, L = Nφ/i, unit henry (1 H = 1 Wb/A = 1 V·s/A). A changing current changes the flux and induces a voltage.
Capacitance. The charge stored per volt, C = q/v, unit farad (1 F = 1 C/V = 1 A·s/V); for parallel plates C = εA/d.

answer.text: Relations, with the passive sign convention (current enters the + terminal):

answer: Energy derivation. For L: p = vi = Li di/dt = d(½Li²)/dt, so the energy stored when the current rises from 0 to i is ½Li². For C: p = Cv dv/dt = d(½Cv²)/dt, giving ½Cv². For R, p = i²R is never negative, so a resistor only absorbs energy.
DC steady state. Nothing changes, so di/dt = 0 gives vL = 0 for any current (a short circuit), and dv/dt = 0 gives iC = 0 for any voltage (an open circuit).

Continuity. If iL jumped in zero time, di/dt and so vL would be infinite; no real source supplies that. So iL(0⁺) = iL(0⁻). In the same way an instant jump of vC needs infinite current, so vC(0⁺) = vC(0⁻). The inductor's voltage and the capacitor's current can jump.

answer.text: Numerical illustration. A 0.5 H inductor carrying 2 A with di/dt = 40 A/s, and a 100 μF capacitor at 10 V with dv/dt = 200 V/s:

answer: Real components. A real coil has winding resistance Rw in series, so at DC it is not a perfect short: a 0.4 H coil with Rw = 5 Ω carrying 2 A drops 10 V and wastes 20 W. A real capacitor leaks a small current and has an equivalent series resistance, so it slowly loses its stored charge. A resistor is linear only within its power rating.
Check. Units: H × A/s = (V·s/A)(A/s) = V, and F × V/s = (A·s/V)(V/s) = A. The inductor's energy rises at Li di/dt = 0.5 × 2 × 40 = 40 W, equal to vLi = 20 × 2 = 40 W.

bank.q: Explain the types of sources: ideal and practical voltage and current sources with their V-I characteristics, and the four dependent sources with their symbols and gain units.
outline: Ideal voltage source: fixed v, any current, zero internal resistance
Ideal current source: fixed i, any voltage, infinite internal resistance
Practical models: V<sub>s</sub> with series R<sub>s</sub>, I<sub>s</sub> with parallel R<sub>p</sub>; v = V<sub>s</sub> − iR<sub>s</sub>
Dependent sources VCVS, VCCS, CCVS, CCCS; diamond symbol; gains μ, g, r, β
Forbidden connections: shorting a voltage source, opening a current source
answer: Independent sources fix their own value. An ideal voltage source keeps v = Vs for any current (symbol: circle with + and −); its characteristic on a v against i graph is a horizontal line, and its internal resistance is zero. An ideal current source keeps i = Is for any voltage (circle with an arrow); its characteristic is a vertical line, and its internal resistance is infinite.
Practical voltage source: Vs in series with Rs, so v = Vs − iRs. Open-circuit voltage Vs; short-circuit current Vs/Rs. The line slopes down with slope −Rs.
Practical current source: Is in parallel with Rp, so i = Is − v/Rp. A good current source has Rp much larger than the load.

answer.text: Worked numbers for a 12 V battery with Rs = 0.5 Ω:
Dependent sources are drawn as diamonds; the output is set by a control voltage vx or current ix elsewhere.

answer: Rules. Never short an ideal voltage source or open an ideal current source: KVL or KCL would need an infinite current or voltage. A source set to zero becomes a short (voltage) or an open (current). A dependent source is active and is never switched off on its own.

Reading the table. The load power rises from 11.5 W to 54 W as the load resistance falls, but the share lost inside rises faster: 0.5 W of 12 W at 1 A, 18 W of 72 W at 6 A. The load power is largest when RL = Rs = 0.5 Ω: i = 12 A, v = 6 V, 72 W in the load and 72 W wasted inside, which the maximum power transfer theorem later explains.
Check. In the table, v × i + i²Rs = 12i in every row: for 6 A, 54 + 6² × 0.5 = 54 + 18 = 72 W = 12 × 6.

bank.q: State Ohm's law, KCL and KVL, and explain the sign conventions used with them. A 12 V supply with 2 Ω in series and a 4 V cell with 4 Ω in series both feed a node A, from which an 8 Ω load goes to the common return. Find all branch currents and verify the power balance.
outline: Ohm's law v = iR, valid for ohmic elements at constant temperature
KCL: Σi = 0 at a node (charge conservation); KVL: Σv = 0 round a closed path (energy conservation)
Reference arrows, entering-positive rule, rise and drop rule
Branch-current equations: one KCL, two KVL; I₁ = 2 A, I₂ = −1 A, I₃ = 1 A
Power: 24 W delivered = 8 + 4 + 8 + 4 W
answer: Ohm's law. For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, v = iR (equivalently i = Gv, G = 1/R in siemens). With the current arrow entering the + terminal, the resistor absorbs p = i²R.

KCL. The algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero: Σi = 0. Mark a reference arrow on every branch, count entering currents positive and leaving negative (or the reverse, consistently). It follows from conservation of charge.

KVL. The algebraic sum of voltages round any closed path is zero: Σv = 0. Walk round in one direction; a − to + crossing is a rise (+), a + to − crossing is a drop (−). For a resistor the + end is where the current arrow enters. It follows from conservation of energy.
Set-up. Let I₁ flow from the 12 V supply into A through 2 Ω, I₂ from the 4 V cell into A through 4 Ω, and I₃ from A down through 8 Ω. The return wire B is the 0 V reference.

answer.text: Equations.
answer.pre:
KCL at A:        I₁ + I₂ − I₃ = 0                   (1)
KVL left loop:   12 − 2I₁ − 8I₃ = 0  →  2I₁ + 8I₃ = 12  (2)
KVL right loop:  4 − 4I₂ − 8I₃ = 0   →  4I₂ + 8I₃ = 4   (3)

answer.text: Solve. Substitute I₃ = I₁ + I₂:

answer: Meaning of the sign. I₂ is negative, so 1 A actually flows from A into the + terminal of the 4 V cell: the supply is charging the cell.
Node voltage. VA = 8 × 1 = 8 V; from the left 12 − 2 × 2 = 8 V; from the right 4 − 4 × (−1) = 8 V. All three agree.

answer.text: A shorter route, as a cross-check. Write KCL once at A in terms of VA, using Ohm's law for each branch current:
answer.pre:
(12 − V<sub>A</sub>)/2 + (4 − V<sub>A</sub>)/4 = V<sub>A</sub>/8
× 8:  48 − 4V<sub>A</sub> + 8 − 2V<sub>A</sub> = V<sub>A</sub>
56 = 7V<sub>A</sub>   →   V<sub>A</sub> = 8 V

answer.text: Power balance.

answer: Check. Absorbed 8 + 4 + 8 + 4 = 24 W equals the 24 W delivered, and KCL holds: 2 + (−1) = 1 A.

bank.q: Define node, junction, branch, loop, mesh, tree, link and cut-set. State how many twigs, links, meshes and independent KCL equations a connected circuit with n nodes and b branches has, and apply the counts to a bridge circuit with four nodes and six branches.
outline: One-line definitions of each term
Twigs n − 1; links b − n + 1; meshes b − n + 1 for a planar circuit
Independent equations: n − 1 KCL and b − n + 1 KVL, total b
Bridge: n = 4, b = 6, 3 twigs, 3 links, 3 meshes, 7 loops
answer: Node: a point (or a whole connected piece of ideal wire) where two or more elements meet. Junction: a node where three or more elements meet. Branch: one element (or one series chain) between two nodes, carrying one current.
Loop: any closed path that does not use a branch twice. Mesh: a loop with no branch inside it, a window pane of a planar drawing.

Tree: a connected set of branches touching every node with no closed path; its branches are twigs. Link (chord): a branch not in the tree. Cut-set: a minimal set of branches whose removal splits the graph into exactly two parts.

answer.text: Counts for a connected graph:
answer.pre:
twigs                  = n − 1
links                  = b − n + 1
meshes (planar)        = b − n + 1
independent KCL        = n − 1
independent KVL        = b − n + 1
total                  = b

answer: Why n − 1 KCL equations. Each branch current leaves one node and enters another, so the n equations add to 0 = 0; one is redundant.
The bridge (A top, B left, C right, D bottom; 20 Ω A-B, 20 Ω A-C, 10 Ω B-C, 2 Ω B-D, 8 Ω C-D, source D-A): n = 4, and every node meets three elements, so all four are junctions; b = 6.
Twigs = 3 (for example the 2 Ω, the 8 Ω and the source, all meeting D); links = 6 − 4 + 1 = 3 (the 20 Ω, 20 Ω and 10 Ω).
Meshes = 3: source-20 Ω-2 Ω, triangle A-B-C and triangle B-C-D. Loops = 7 (four triangles and three four-node paths); the outer path source-20 Ω (A-C)-8 Ω is a loop but not a mesh.

Open and short cases. If the 10 Ω cross arm is removed (open), b = 5 and m = 5 − 4 + 1 = 2; B and C now meet only two elements each, so they are nodes but not junctions. If instead the 10 Ω is shorted by a wire, B and C merge (n = 3) and the 10 Ω drops out (b = 5), so m = 5 − 3 + 1 = 3.
Convention. Some textbooks count only junctions as nodes and each series chain as one branch. Either convention gives the same mesh count, provided it is used throughout one answer.
Check. KCL 3 + KVL 3 = 6 = b, so the circuit needs exactly six independent equations for its six branch currents.

bank.q: A 12 V source drives 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 10 Ω in series. Find the current, the voltage across each resistor by the voltage-divider rule, and the power taken by each resistor. What extra series resistance would limit the current to 0.4 A, and what would the 10 Ω resistor then see?
outline: R<sub>eq</sub> = 20 Ω
Divider: 2.4 V, 3.6 V, 6 V
Powers 1.44 W, 2.16 W, 3.6 W; total 7.2 W
For 0.4 A: total 30 Ω, add 10 Ω; the 10 Ω sees 4 V
answer: Equivalent. Series resistances add: Req = 4 + 6 + 10 = 20 Ω.

Sketch. One loop: the 12 V source with + at the top, then the 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 10 Ω in a row, back to the − terminal. The current arrow leaves the + terminal, and each resistor has its + mark where the current enters.
Current. I = V/Req = 12/20 = 0.6 A, the same in every resistor, since there is only one path.

answer.text: Voltage divider, Vx = V Rx/Req:
Powers, p = I²R:

answer: The largest resistor takes the largest share of both voltage and power, because in series every resistor carries the same current. The divider rule is just Ohm's law twice: I = V/R<sub>eq</sub>, then V<sub>x</sub> = IR<sub>x</sub> = VR<sub>x</sub>/R<sub>eq</sub>.

answer.text: Limiting the current to 0.4 A.
answer.pre:
R<sub>total</sub> = 12 V / 0.4 A = 30 Ω
extra series R = 30 − 20 = 10 Ω
V<sub>10</sub> = 12 × 10/30 = 4 V   (was 6 V)

answer: Common slip. Using the divider with the wrong total (for example 12 × 10/16, leaving out the 4 Ω) gives 7.5 V for the 10 Ω; the total in the denominator must include every resistor that carries the same current.
Adding series resistance lowers the current and therefore every voltage share of the original resistors; the new 10 Ω takes 4 V of the 12 V. The source now delivers 12 × 0.4 = 4.8 W instead of 7.2 W.
Check. KVL: 2.4 + 3.6 + 6 = 12 V. Power: 1.44 + 2.16 + 3.6 = 7.2 W = 12 V × 0.6 A delivered by the source. With the extra resistor: 0.4 × (4 + 6 + 10 + 10) = 1.6 + 2.4 + 4 + 4 = 12 V.

bank.q: Resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are in parallel across a 9 V source. Use the current-divider rule to find each branch current, verify with Ohm's law and KCL, and find the power in each. A 2 Ω resistor is then added in parallel: find the new branch currents with the conductance form of the divider.
outline: R<sub>eq</sub> = 6 ∥ 3 = 2 Ω
KCL 1.5 + 3 = 4.5 A; powers 13.5 W and 27 W
With 2 Ω added: G = 1 S, I = 9 A; 1.5 A, 3 A, 4.5 A
answer: Sketch. The 9 V source with the 6 Ω and the 3 Ω connected across the same two wires; the source current splits at the top node into I₆ and I₃ and recombines at the bottom node.
Equivalent. Product over sum: Req = 6 × 3/(6 + 3) = 18/9 = 2 Ω. It is smaller than the smaller branch, 3 Ω, as every parallel equivalent must be.

answer.text: Why the divider has the other resistance on top. Both branches share V = I Req:
answer.pre:
V  = I R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂)
I₁ = V/R₁ = I R₂/(R₁ + R₂)
I₂ = V/R₂ = I R₁/(R₁ + R₂)

answer: Total current. I = 9/2 = 4.5 A.

answer.text: Current divider (the other resistance on top):

answer: Ohm's law check. Both branches have the full 9 V: 9/6 = 1.5 A and 9/3 = 3 A. The smaller resistor carries twice the current of the larger, since 6/3 = 2.
KCL check. 1.5 + 3 = 4.5 A, the source current.
Powers. p = V²/R: 81/6 = 13.5 W in the 6 Ω and 81/3 = 27 W in the 3 Ω; total 40.5 W = 9 × 4.5.

answer.text: Third resistor, conductance form Ik = I Gk/Gtotal:

answer: Because the source is an ideal 9 V source, adding a branch leaves the old branch currents unchanged; only the source current rises, from 4.5 A to 9 A. With a practical source the terminal voltage would sag and every branch current would fall.
Check. 1.5 + 3 + 4.5 = 9 A. In parallel the smaller resistance takes more current and more power; in series it would take less.

bank.q: Convert a 20 V source with 5 Ω in series into its current-source equivalent, and use it to find the current, voltage and power of a 10 Ω load. Verify with the original circuit and compare the power delivered by the ideal source in the two forms.
outline: I<sub>s</sub> = 20/5 = 4 A in parallel with 5 Ω, arrow to the old + terminal
Current divider: 4 × 5/15 = 1.333 A
Ideal-source powers 26.67 W and 53.33 W differ
Use: an extra 2 A source across the terminals merges to 6 A, giving 2 A in the load
answer: Transform. Is = Vs/R = 20/5 = 4 A, in parallel with the same 5 Ω. The arrow points to the terminal that was the + of the 20 V source.

Why these values. Both forms must give the same open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current. Open circuit: the voltage form gives 20 V; the current form gives 4 × 5 = 20 V. Short circuit: the voltage form gives 20/5 = 4 A out of the + terminal; the current form sends its whole 4 A through the short, so the arrow must point to that same terminal.
Load in the current form. The 5 Ω and the 10 Ω load are in parallel across the 4 A source. Current divider: IL = 4 × 5/(5 + 10) = 20/15 = 1.333 A.
Load voltage and power. VL = 1.333 × 10 = 13.33 V; PL = 1.333² × 10 = 17.78 W.
Direct check. In the voltage form the 5 Ω and 10 Ω are in series: I = 20/15 = 1.333 A and VL = 13.33 V. The same.

answer.text: Source powers.

answer: Meaning. The two models are equivalent only at the terminals: the load sees 13.33 V and 1.333 A either way, but the power inside the model is different. Never use a transformed model to find the losses inside a real source.

answer.text: Why the current form helps. Suppose an ideal 2 A current source is also connected across the same two terminals, pushing current towards the + terminal. In the current form the two sources are simply in parallel and add:
answer.pre:
4 A + 2 A = 6 A in parallel with 5 Ω
I<sub>L</sub> = 6 × 5/(5 + 10) = 2 A,   V<sub>L</sub> = 20 V
check by KCL at the top node:  (20 − V)/5 + 2 = V/10  →  V = 20 V

answer: Check. Each form balances: 8.89 + 17.78 = 26.67 W and 35.56 + 17.78 = 53.33 W (to rounding).

bank.q: A bridge has a 27 V source between D and A, R<sub>AB</sub> = 12 Ω, R<sub>AC</sub> = 12 Ω, R<sub>BC</sub> = 24 Ω, R<sub>BD</sub> = 3 Ω and R<sub>CD</sub> = 12 Ω. Using star-delta transformation, find the resistance seen by the source, the source current and the current in every resistor.
outline: Balance check: 12/3 ≠ 12/12, so the cross arm carries current
Delta A-B-C to star: R<sub>A</sub> = 3 Ω, R<sub>B</sub> = 6 Ω, R<sub>C</sub> = 6 Ω
Paths 9 Ω and 18 Ω in parallel: 6 Ω; total 9 Ω; I = 3 A
Split 2 A and 1 A; V<sub>B</sub> = 6 V, V<sub>C</sub> = 12 V
Original delta currents 1.75 A, 1.25 A, 0.25 A; KCL checks
answer: Balance check. RAB/RBD = 12/3 = 4 and RAC/RCD = 12/12 = 1. Not equal, so the 24 Ω cross arm carries current and simple reduction is blocked.

answer.text: Delta A-B-C to star (centre N), S = 12 + 24 + 12 = 48 Ω:
answer.pre:
R<sub>A</sub> = R<sub>AB</sub>R<sub>CA</sub>/S = 12 × 12/48 = 3 Ω
R<sub>B</sub> = R<sub>AB</sub>R<sub>BC</sub>/S = 12 × 24/48 = 6 Ω
R<sub>C</sub> = R<sub>BC</sub>R<sub>CA</sub>/S = 24 × 12/48 = 6 Ω

answer: Check of the star: P = 3 × 6 + 6 × 6 + 6 × 3 = 72; P/RC = 12 = RAB, P/RA = 24 = RBC, P/RB = 12 = RCA.
Reduce. Path N-B-D: 6 + 3 = 9 Ω. Path N-C-D: 6 + 12 = 18 Ω. In parallel: 9 × 18/27 = 6 Ω. Add RA: Req = 3 + 6 = 9 Ω.
Source current. I = 27/9 = 3 A.
Split at N. N-B-D carries 3 × 18/27 = 2 A, N-C-D carries 3 × 9/27 = 1 A. With D at 0 V: VB = 2 × 3 = 6 V, VC = 1 × 12 = 12 V, VA = 27 V.

answer.text: Currents in the original circuit:

answer: The star-arm currents (3 A, 2 A, 1 A) are not the currents of the delta resistors; those come from the node voltages, as in the table.

Choice of group. Converting the delta A-B-C was the natural choice because its star arms land in series with the 3 Ω and 12 Ω arms. Converting the star at B (12 Ω, 24 Ω, 3 Ω meeting at B) to a delta would also work but leaves more parallel pairs to combine.

Draw the oriented graph, choose the tree {1, 2, 4, 6}, write the fundamental tie-set and cut-set matrices, and find all branch currents from the tie-set equations.

Tie-set matrix B with one row per link; cut-set matrix Q with one row per twig

svg.aria: Oriented graph of the ladder: node 0 at the bottom, nodes 1 to 4 along the top. Tree branches 1, 2, 4, 6 drawn solid; links 3, 5, 7 dashed from the top nodes down to node 0.

answer.text: Tie-set matrix B (each loop oriented like its link; columns are branches 1 to 7):
Cut-set matrix Q (each cut oriented like its twig):

answer: Sign rules used. In B an entry is +1 when the branch arrow agrees with the loop, which is oriented like its link; every twig here lies along the path 0-1-2-3-4 in its own arrow direction, so all entries are +1. In Q an entry is +1 when the branch crosses the cut in the same direction as the twig; each shunt link points down to node 0, against the twig, hence −1. As a check, every row of B times every row of Q gives 0.
Branch currents from link currents (i = Bᵀ IL): i₃ = I₃, i₅ = I₅, i₇ = I₇, i₆ = I₇, i₄ = I₅ + I₇, i₁ = i₂ = I₃ + I₅ + I₇.

answer.text: Tie-set (KVL) equations. Branch voltage is the drop along the arrow; the source branch has v₁ = −18 V.
answer.pre:
link 3:  −18 + 1·i₂ + 1·i₃ = 0              →  2I₃ +  I₅ +  I₇ = 18
link 5:  −18 + i₂ + 2i₄ + 4i₅ = 0           →   I₃ + 7I₅ + 3I₇ = 18
link 7:  −18 + i₂ + 2i₄ + 1·i₆ + 3i₇ = 0    →   I₃ + 3I₅ + 7I₇ = 18

answer.text: Solve.
answer.pre:
(link 5) − (link 7):  4I₅ − 4I₇ = 0  →  I₅ = I₇
link 3:  2I₃ + 2I₅ = 18   →  I₃ = 9 − I₅
link 5:  (9 − I₅) + 10I₅ = 18  →  I₅ = 1 A
I₇ = 1 A,  I₃ = 8 A

answer: All branch currents. i₁ = i₂ = 10 A, i₃ = 8 A, i₄ = 2 A, i₅ = 1 A, i₆ = 1 A, i₇ = 1 A.
Check by reduction. From the far end: 1 + 3 = 4 Ω; ∥ 4 Ω = 2 Ω; + 2 Ω = 4 Ω; ∥ 1 Ω = 0.8 Ω; + 1 Ω = 1.8 Ω; 18/1.8 = 10 A, the source current found above.

bank.q: A 12 V source with 2 Ω in series feeds node A. From A, a 6 Ω resistor carrying current i<sub>x</sub> goes to the return, and a current-controlled current source of value 2i<sub>x</sub> draws current from A to the return. Find the voltage of A, i<sub>x</sub> and the source current; explain why the dependent source cannot be treated as an independent one, and show what resistance it behaves like.
outline: KCL at A with the control written as i<sub>x</sub> = V<sub>A</sub>/6
V<sub>A</sub> = 6 V, i<sub>x</sub> = 1 A, CCCS 2 A, source current 3 A
Treating 2i<sub>x</sub> as fixed gives a wrong circuit when anything changes
The CCCS acts as a 3 Ω resistor; power balance 36 W
answer: Unknowns. Take the return as 0 V and VA as the unknown. The control is ix = VA/6 (Ohm's law on the 6 Ω).

answer.text: KCL at A (current in = currents out):
answer.pre:
(12 − V<sub>A</sub>)/2 = V<sub>A</sub>/6 + 2i<sub>x</sub>
                = V<sub>A</sub>/6 + 2V<sub>A</sub>/6 = V<sub>A</sub>/2
12 − V<sub>A</sub> = V<sub>A</sub>   →   V<sub>A</sub> = 6 V

answer: Currents. ix = 6/6 = 1 A; the CCCS carries 2ix = 2 A; the source current is (12 − 6)/2 = 3 A. KCL: 1 + 2 = 3 A.
Branch-current check (KVL). Round the source, 2 Ω and 6 Ω: 12 − 2 × 3 − 6 × 1 = 0.

answer.text: Power balance.

answer: Why not independent. The CCCS value depends on ix, which depends on VA. If the source voltage changes to 24 V, the same KCL gives VA = 12 V, ix = 2 A and a CCCS of 4 A, not 2 A. Writing it as a fixed 2 A would give (24 − V)/2 = V/6 + 2, so V = 15 V, which is wrong. So keep the control variable as an unknown and add its control equation.
Equivalent resistance. The CCCS carries 2ix = 2VA/6 = VA/3 with VA across it: it behaves like a 3 Ω resistor. Then 6 ∥ 3 = 2 Ω, and the source sees 2 + 2 = 4 Ω: 12/4 = 3 A, as found.

answer.text: Effect of the gain. Let the CCCS be k·ix. KCL × 6 gives:
answer.pre:
3(12 − V<sub>A</sub>) = V<sub>A</sub> + kV<sub>A</sub>   →   V<sub>A</sub> = 36/(4 + k)
k = 0:  V<sub>A</sub> = 9 V     k = 2:  V<sub>A</sub> = 6 V     k = 8:  V<sub>A</sub> = 3 V

answer: A larger gain draws more current from A and pulls V<sub>A</sub> down. With a negative gain (the source pushing current into A) the equivalent resistance 6/k becomes negative; at k = −4 the denominator vanishes and the circuit has no finite solution. Dependent sources can therefore make a circuit behave in ways no set of positive resistors can, which is another reason to keep their control equations explicit.
Check. With 24 V the equivalent still gives 24/4 = 6 A and VA = 24 − 12 = 12 V, matching the KCL result above.

bank.q: An 18 V source feeds 3 Ω in series with a parallel pair: 6 Ω in one branch and 2 Ω + 4 Ω in series in the other. Find the current and voltage of the 4 Ω resistor. Compare series-parallel reduction with the dividers against writing KCL and KVL for every branch, and justify the shorter route.
outline: Current divider: equal branches, 1.5 A each
V<sub>4</sub> = 6 V
Branch method needs 4 unknowns; reduction needs no simultaneous equations
Check with KVL and KCL
answer: Identify the groups. The 2 Ω and 4 Ω share one current (nothing else at their joint), so they are in series: 6 Ω. That 6 Ω chain and the 6 Ω branch share the same two nodes, so they are in parallel.

answer.text: Reduction.

answer: Divider. Current divider between the two 6 Ω branches: each takes 3 × 6/12 = 1.5 A. Voltage divider instead: the pair has 18 × 3/6 = 9 V, and inside the 2-4 chain the 4 Ω takes 9 × 4/6 = 6 V.
Answer. The 4 Ω carries 1.5 A and has 1.5 × 4 = 6 V across it.

Branch-equation route. Unknown currents: the 3 Ω (I), the 6 Ω (I₁) and the 2-4 chain (I₂), with one KCL (I = I₁ + I₂) and two KVL equations (18 = 3I + 6I₁ and 6I₁ = 6I₂). Solving three simultaneous equations gives the same I = 3 A, I₁ = I₂ = 1.5 A, but takes more steps and more chances of a sign slip.

Choice. When every group is plainly series or parallel, reduction plus one divider is shorter: no simultaneous equations, and each line is a single formula. When a bridge or a second source prevents reduction, the branch, mesh or nodal equations are the right tool.

What if a branch fails? If the 6 Ω branch opens, reduction gives at once 3 + 2 + 4 = 9 Ω, I = 2 A and V4 = 8 V: one line, where the branch method would need its equations rewritten. Reduction makes such fault questions quick, which is why some syllabi pair it with troubleshooting.

bank.q: Evaluate the statement: "A star-delta transformation changes the power dissipated in the network." Use terminal equivalence and a numerical example to justify your answer.
outline: The transformation keeps terminal voltages and currents
So total power into the group, ΣV<sub>k</sub>I<sub>k</sub>, is unchanged
Power in each resistor differs
Example: the 27 V bridge, 57 W in both delta and star
Verdict: false for the total, true for individual resistors
answer: What equivalence means. A star and a delta are equivalent when, for every set of terminal voltages, the currents into terminals A, B and C are the same. Nothing is promised about the inside.

Total power. The power entering any three-terminal group is p = VAIA + VBIB + VCIC (currents entering, potentials from a common reference). Equal terminal voltages and currents give equal total power, so for resistors the total heat is the same.

Individual powers. The resistor values and their currents are different, so the heat in any one resistor is different. There is not even a one-to-one pairing: a delta side joins two terminals, while a star arm joins a terminal to a centre node that the delta does not have.

answer.text: Example: the bridge with 27 V, delta 12 Ω (A-B), 24 Ω (B-C), 12 Ω (C-A) and star 3 Ω, 6 Ω, 6 Ω; terminal voltages VA = 27 V, VB = 6 V, VC = 12 V.

answer: Terminal check. Currents entering the group: 3 A at A, −2 A at B, −1 A at C. Total power = 27 × 3 + 6 × (−2) + 12 × (−1) = 81 − 12 − 12 = 57 W, the same as both totals.

answer.text: Equivalence test between pairs of terminals (third terminal open):

answer: Rest of the circuit. Outside the group nothing changes either: the 3 Ω and 12 Ω arms carry 2 A and 1 A and absorb 12 W each in both versions, and the source delivers 81 W = 57 + 12 + 12 W.

Verdict. The statement is false for the total power, which the transformation preserves, and true only for the power in individual resistors. Use the transformed network for terminal quantities and totals; go back to the original for any resistor inside the group.

bank.q: A practical voltage source is V<sub>s</sub> in series with R<sub>s</sub>, and a practical current source is I<sub>s</sub> in parallel with R<sub>p</sub>. Derive the conditions for the two to be equivalent at their terminals, test them with a 9 V source of 2 Ω, and discuss the limits of the model.
outline: v = V<sub>s</sub> − iR<sub>s</sub> and v = I<sub>s</sub>R<sub>p</sub> − iR<sub>p</sub>
Equal for all i only if R<sub>p</sub> = R<sub>s</sub> and V<sub>s</sub> = I<sub>s</sub>R<sub>s</sub>
9 V, 2 Ω ↔ 4.5 A, 2 Ω; same output for 1 Ω and 7 Ω loads
Limits: ideal sources, internal power, nonlinear real sources, load inside
answer: Voltage form. KVL: v = Vs − iRs, where i is the current delivered at the + terminal.
Current form. KCL at the top terminal: Is = i + v/Rp, so v = IsRp − iRp.

Condition. Two straight lines in i are identical for every i only when their slopes and intercepts match: Rp = Rs and Vs = IsRs. Equivalently, both have open-circuit voltage Vs and short-circuit current Is.

answer.text: Test: 9 V with 2 Ω becomes 4.5 A in parallel with 2 Ω.

answer: Limits. (1) An ideal source cannot be transformed: Rs = 0 gives an infinite Is, and an ideal current source has no finite parallel resistance. (2) The equivalence is external only: with the 1 Ω load the voltage form loses 3² × 2 = 18 W inside, the current form loses 3²/2 = 4.5 W, so internal heating cannot be read from the transformed model. (3) A real battery's EMF and internal resistance change with charge and temperature, so the straight line holds only over a range. (4) The load, or any element whose current is wanted, must stay outside the part being transformed.

answer.text: Using the equivalence. Put the 9 V, 2 Ω source in parallel with a 6 V, 3 Ω source (both + at the top) across a 1.8 Ω load:

answer: Each practical source became a current source so that parallel sources could simply be added; the merged source was then turned back into a voltage form so that the load current came from one series loop.
Check. Both forms give an open-circuit voltage of 9 V (4.5 × 2) and a short-circuit current of 4.5 A (9/2).

bank.q: Using graph theory, explain how a tree selects independent KVL and KCL equations, and show that tie-sets and cut-sets give the same numbers of independent equations as mesh and nodal analysis. Illustrate with the bridge circuit (36 V source; 20 Ω A-B, 20 Ω A-C, 10 Ω B-C, 2 Ω B-D, 8 Ω C-D) and solve it.
outline: Tree: n − 1 twigs; links b − n + 1
Each link gives one fundamental loop with a link no other loop has: independent KVL
Each twig gives one fundamental cut-set with a twig no other cut has: independent KCL
Mesh count b − n + 1 for planar circuits; nodal count n − 1
Bridge: tree {4, 5, 6}; I₁ = 1.6 A, I₂ = 1.4 A, I₃ = 0.4 A; cut-set check
answer: Tree and its complement. For a connected graph a tree has n − 1 twigs and leaves b − n + 1 links. Twig voltages fix every node potential (each node is reached from the reference along the tree), and link currents fix every branch current.

Independent KVL. Each link plus its tree path forms one fundamental loop. Each loop contains its own link and no other, so no loop equation is a combination of the others: there are b − n + 1 independent KVL equations, B v = 0.

Independent KCL. Removing each twig splits the tree into two parts; the twig and the links joining the parts form a fundamental cut-set. Each contains its own twig and no other, so the n − 1 cut-set equations, Q i = 0, are independent.

Comparison. Mesh analysis writes one equation per window of a planar drawing; Euler's formula gives b − n + 1 windows, the same as the number of links. Nodal analysis writes n − 1 equations; the same as the number of twigs. Tie-set analysis also works for non-planar circuits, where meshes are not defined.

answer.text: Bridge graph. Branches 1: A→B, 2: A→C, 3: C→B, 4: B→D, 5: C→D, 6: D→A (source). n = 4, b = 6. Tree {4, 5, 6}, links {1, 2, 3}.
Equations (i₄ = I₁ + I₃, i₅ = I₂ − I₃, i₆ = I₁ + I₂; source branch v₆ = −36 V):
answer.pre:
link 1:  20I₁ + 2(I₁ + I₃) − 36 = 0           →  22I₁ + 2I₃ = 36
link 2:  20I₂ + 8(I₂ − I₃) − 36 = 0           →  28I₂ − 8I₃ = 36
link 3:  10I₃ + 2(I₁ + I₃) − 8(I₂ − I₃) = 0   →  2I₁ − 8I₂ + 20I₃ = 0

answer.text: Solve.

answer: Branch currents. i₁ = 1.6 A, i₂ = 1.4 A, i₃ = 0.4 A, i₄ = 2 A, i₅ = 1 A, i₆ = 3 A.

answer.text: Cut-set check (Q i = 0):
Nodal comparison. With D as reference the source fixes VA = 36 V, so nodal analysis needs only VB and VC:
answer.pre:
at B:  (36 − V<sub>B</sub>)/20 + (V<sub>C</sub> − V<sub>B</sub>)/10 = V<sub>B</sub>/2
at C:  (36 − V<sub>C</sub>)/20 = (V<sub>C</sub> − V<sub>B</sub>)/10 + V<sub>C</sub>/8
V<sub>B</sub> = 4 V, V<sub>C</sub> = 8 V:  1.6 + 0.4 = 2 ✓   1.4 = 0.4 + 1 ✓

answer: Count check. 3 tie-set + 3 cut-set = 6 = b equations, the same as 3 mesh + 3 nodal equations for this planar circuit (the voltage source removes one nodal unknown, as it fixes VA). The source sees 36/3 = 12 Ω, the value star-delta reduction gives.

glossary.def: An element that can deliver net energy to a circuit, such as an independent or dependent source.
A single element (or one series chain) between two nodes, carrying one current.
Charge stored per volt, C = q/v, in farads.
The reciprocal of resistance, G = 1/R, in siemens (S).
The rule that splits a current between parallel branches in inverse proportion to their resistances.
A minimal set of branches whose removal splits a connected graph into exactly two parts; it gives one KCL equation.
Three resistors connected in a closed triangle between three terminals.
A source whose voltage or current is a fixed multiple of a voltage or current elsewhere in the circuit.
A source that keeps its current fixed whatever the terminal voltage; infinite internal resistance.
A source that keeps its terminal voltage fixed whatever the current; zero internal resistance.
A node-by-branch matrix with +1 where a branch leaves a node and −1 where it enters.
Flux linkage per ampere of a coil, L = Nφ/i, in henries.
A node where three or more elements meet.
The algebraic sum of the currents at a node is zero.
The algebraic sum of the voltages round any closed path is zero.
A branch not in the chosen tree, also called a chord; each link closes one fundamental loop.
Any closed path in a circuit that does not use a branch twice.
A loop with no branch inside it; a window pane of a planar drawing.
A point, or a connected piece of ideal wire, where two or more elements meet.
For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, v = iR.
A break carrying zero current for any voltage (R → ∞).
Current reference entering the + terminal, so that p = vi is the power absorbed.
A circuit that can be drawn on paper with no branch crossing another.
An ideal source with an internal resistance, in series for a voltage source or in parallel for a current source.
A connection with zero voltage for any current (R = 0).
Replacing V<sub>s</sub> in series with R by I<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>/R in parallel with R, or the reverse.
Three resistors joined at a common centre node, with their free ends as the terminals.
The branches of a fundamental loop: one link plus its tree path; it gives one KVL equation.
A connected set of branches touching every node with no closed path; its branches are twigs.
The rule that shares a voltage between series resistors in proportion to their resistances.
